Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Necrotizing sialometaplasia

One case report described complete healing of bilateral palatal lesions within two weeks and no relapse at three months; without a comparator, the cause of healing is uncertain.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One case report described complete healing of bilateral palatal lesions within two weeks and no relapse at three months; without a comparator, the cause of healing is uncertain.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Oral > Necrotizing sialometaplasia category contains one unique publication, a human case report from Brazil. No controlled clinical study, animal experiment, review, or laboratory study was listed. The single report cannot estimate how often lesions would heal without PBM.

Human and clinical evidence

Leite and colleagues described one 32-year-old man with bilateral crater-like palatal lesions. The clinical diagnosis was made after a recent illness, and the lesions had been present for about two weeks before PBM. The authors reported complete wound healing within two weeks of treatment and no complication or relapse at the three-month follow-up (Leite et al. 2020). There was no untreated or sham-treated comparison, and the report does not establish that PBM caused the healing.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal evidence was identified for necrotizing sialometaplasia.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell, tissue, blood, or ex-vivo study was identified for this indication.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The case used a 660-nm red diode laser at 30 mW, with 1.1 J/cm² reported per point and 100 seconds per point. Four sessions were delivered over two weeks. These details describe one patient and one treatment schedule; the report does not compare doses or show whether the same schedule would work in other patients.

Interpretation

The report documents healing after PBM but offers very little evidence about treatment effect. Because the condition may resolve naturally, the case cannot distinguish an effect of light from spontaneous recovery, the course of the lesion, or other influences.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for healing of necrotizing sialometaplasia after PBM because evidence is limited to one uncontrolled case
Publications and records1 unique title

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The only direct record is a single case without a comparator, and this lesion can resolve during its natural course. Healing followed treatment, but the report cannot separate a treatment effect from spontaneous recovery or other care. Replicated cases with predefined assessment and a suitable comparison would be needed before drawing a stronger conclusion.
